chapters.title: Diocletian and Constantine
chapters.body:
[[diocletian|Diocletian]] ruled for twenty-one years and then did what no emperor had done: he abdicated and retired to grow cabbages in his palace at Spalatum (Split). His reign and that of [[constantine_i|Constantine]] created the late Roman state, larger, more hierarchical, more expensive and more intrusive than the Principate, and ended it as a Christian empire with a new capital. The two reigns are often treated as a single project, but Constantine both completed and dismantled Diocletian's system, and the sources for them are partisan in opposite directions: Lactantius' On the Deaths of the Persecutors and Eusebius' Life of Constantine are Christian polemic, Zosimus and parts of Aurelius Victor pagan.

Diocletian's first problem was that no emperor could be everywhere. In 285-286 he made his comrade [[maximian|Maximian]] first Caesar and then Augustus in the West; in 293 each Augustus adopted a Caesar, [[constantius_i|Constantius]] in the West and [[galerius|Galerius]] in the East, creating the college of four modern scholars call the Tetrarchy. The emperors took the divine patrons Jupiter (Iovius) and Hercules (Herculius), held court at new residences (Trier, Milan, Sirmium, Nicomedia, Antioch) rather than Rome, and were portrayed as interchangeable, as in the porphyry group now on the corner of San Marco in Venice. Court ceremonial grew: subjects prostrated themselves (adoratio) and kissed the emperor's purple robe. The college fought on every front with success. Constantius and his prefect Asclepiodotus recovered Britain from Allectus in 296, and Galerius, after an initial defeat, captured the Persian king Narseh's harem in 297; the Peace of Nisibis (298) gave Rome five regions beyond the Tigris.

The administrative reforms were radical. The provinces, about fifty under the Severans, were divided into roughly a hundred, grouped into a dozen dioceses under vicarii responsible to the praetorian prefects. Civil and military authority were separated: governors judged and taxed, while frontier commanders (duces) led the troops. The army grew substantially (Lactantius, absurdly, says fourfold); modern estimates of 400,000 to 500,000 men are plausible. To pay for it, taxation was reorganised on a new basis: assessment units of land (iugum) and of persons (caput), revised in periodic censuses and announced in an annual budget (indictio), from 312 in fifteen-year cycles. Most of it was collected in kind, as the army required. Diocletian also attempted monetary reform, with a new gold coin, a fine silver argenteus and large bronze nummi. In 301 a currency edict at Aphrodisias doubled the face value of certain coins, and the Edict on Maximum Prices fixed prices and wages for over a thousand items, from a pound of pork (12 denarii) to a lawyer's fee and a camel driver's wage, on pain of death. It failed: goods disappeared from the markets, and the edict was quietly ignored. But dozens of inscribed fragments survive, mostly from the Greek East, and form one of our best sources for late Roman economic life.

Diocletian's religious conservatism produced the last and greatest persecution. Edicts beginning on 23-24 February 303 ordered churches destroyed, scriptures surrendered and Christians stripped of rank; further edicts required clergy and then all inhabitants to sacrifice. Enforcement varied enormously: harsh under Galerius and Maximinus Daia in the East, minimal under Constantius in Gaul and Britain. Diocletian and Maximian abdicated together on 1 May 305, and Galerius and Constantius became Augusti with new Caesars, Severus and Maximinus Daia, chosen over the sons of Maximian and Constantius.

The system broke on dynasty. When Constantius died at York on 25 July 306, his army proclaimed his son Constantine; in Rome Maxentius ([[maxentius|Maxentius]]), son of Maximian, seized power in October with the support of the praetorians and the Roman people, angered by plans to tax Italy. Over the next six years as many as six men claimed the title Augustus. Galerius, dying in 311, issued an edict of toleration admitting the failure of persecution. In 312 Constantine invaded Italy and defeated Maxentius at the [[battle_of_milvian_bridge|Milvian Bridge]] on 28 October, his troops (according to Lactantius) bearing a Christian sign on their shields after a dream; Eusebius later reported Constantine's own account of a cross of light in the sky with the words 'by this conquer'. Constantine disbanded the praetorian guard.

Constantine's conversion is one of the most debated events in history. The sincerity question is perhaps unanswerable; what matters is what he did. From 312 he favoured the church with tax exemptions for clergy, the right of bishops to judge civil cases (episcopalis audientia), money, and buildings, starting with the Lateran basilica in Rome. In 313 he and his eastern ally [[licinius|Licinius]] agreed a policy of religious freedom and restitution of church property (the so-called Edict of Milan, actually a letter of Licinius issued at Nicomedia). He involved himself in church disputes at once: the Donatist schism in Africa, over clergy who had handed over scriptures in the persecution, was referred to councils at Rome (313) and Arles (314). In 321 Sunday became a legal day of rest. His coins showed Sol Invictus until around 320, and pagan cult was not banned, though some temples were stripped of treasure in the 330s.

He was also ruthless. Wars with Licinius in 316 and 324, ending at Adrianople and Chrysopolis, made him sole emperor. In 325 he summoned some 250 to 300 bishops to Nicaea to resolve the controversy over the teaching of Arius, an Alexandrian priest who held that the Son was created by the Father. The council adopted a creed declaring the Son 'of the same substance' (homoousios) as the Father and fixed a common date for Easter. In 326 Constantine executed his eldest son Crispus and soon afterward his wife Fausta, for reasons the sources do not explain. His mother Helena's pilgrimage to Palestine and the building of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre made Jerusalem a Christian holy city.

The new capital was the most durable act of the reign. Constantinople, founded on the site of Byzantium in November 324 and dedicated on 11 May 330, stood at the junction of Europe and Asia, the Danube and Euphrates fronts. It received a senate (of lower rank at first), a free grain distribution, a hippodrome, and statues looted from the cities of the East; within two centuries it was the largest city in the Mediterranean.

Constantine's other reforms reshaped the state. He created a gold coin, the solidus, struck at 72 to the Roman pound, which kept its weight and purity for seven centuries. He divided the army into frontier troops (limitanei) and a mobile field army (comitatenses) under new generals (magistri peditum and equitum), removing military command from the praetorian prefects, who became regional civil administrators. He opened high office to a new aristocracy of service and enlarged the senatorial order. Critics, ancient and modern, accused him of weakening the frontiers, bloating the court and overtaxing; the chrysargyron, a tax in gold on traders, was notoriously resented. He was baptised on his deathbed by the Arian-leaning Eusebius of Nicomedia and died near Nicomedia on 22 May 337. He was buried in Constantinople in a church among cenotaphs of the twelve apostles. The empire he left was Christian at the top and still overwhelmingly pagan below.
chapters.historiography: Burckhardt (1853) saw Constantine as a calculating politician exploiting religion; Baynes and later Barnes (Constantine and Eusebius, 1981) argued for a genuine and early conversion with consistent pro-Christian policy; Van Dam and Lenski stress Constantine's negotiation with traditional elites and the ambiguities of his religious language, and debate how much of Eusebius' Life can be trusted. On the Tetrarchy, scholars dispute whether Diocletian had a coherent system (Barnes, Corcoran) or improvised (Rees, Kolb's 'Diocletian und die Erste Tetrarchie'). The scale of army growth, the nature of the capitatio-iugatio system (Cerati, Carrié) and the effectiveness of the price edict are long-running debates, as is whether late Roman taxation was more oppressive than earlier (Jones versus Wickham).
reading: Barnes, Constantine and Eusebius (1981)
Barnes, The New Empire of Diocletian and Constantine (1982)
Corcoran, The Empire of the Tetrarchs (rev. ed. 2000)
Lenski (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to the Age of Constantine (rev. ed. 2012)
Van Dam, The Roman Revolution of Constantine (2007)
Jones, The Later Roman Empire 284-602 (1964)
Potter, Constantine the Emperor (2013)

chapters.title: The Fourth Century and the Christianisation of the Empire
chapters.body:
The fourth century is unusually well lit. Ammianus Marcellinus, a Greek-speaking officer from Antioch writing in Latin in the 380s and 390s, wrote the last great Latin history in the tradition of Tacitus, and its surviving books cover 353-378 with the eye of a participant. The Theodosian Code of 438 preserves over 2,500 imperial laws from Constantine onwards. Christian writers (Athanasius, Basil, the two Gregories, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine) and pagan ones (Libanius, Themistius, Symmachus, Julian himself) leave thousands of letters, sermons and speeches. The great story they tell is the transformation of a Roman world with a Christian emperor into a Christian Roman world.

Constantine's death was followed by a massacre of his half-brothers and nephews in the summer of 337, leaving his three sons to divide the empire. Constantine II was killed invading the territory of his brother Constans in 340; Constans was murdered in 350 by the usurper Magnentius. [[constantius_ii|Constantius II]], who had held the East against Shapur II ([[shapur_ii|Shapur II]]) in a long war of sieges (Nisibis repelled three Persian attacks, in 337/338, 346 and 350), defeated Magnentius at Mursa in 351, a battle in which some 54,000 men are said to have died, and reunified the empire. Constantius was a committed Christian who backed the 'homoian' compromise (the Son 'like' the Father) against the Nicene party led by Athanasius of Alexandria, who was exiled five times between 335 and 366. Councils at Ariminum and Seleucia (359) briefly imposed it. Constantius also legislated against sacrifice and ordered temples closed, though enforcement was patchy; on his visit to Rome in 357 he removed the Altar of Victory from the Senate house but admired the temples and kept the pagan priesthoods filled.

His cousin [[julian|Julian]], spared in 337 as a child, educated in Greek philosophy and secretly converted to the old gods, was made Caesar in Gaul in 355. He proved a gifted general, defeating the Alamanni at Strasbourg in 357. Proclaimed Augustus by his troops at Paris in 360, he was marching against Constantius when the latter died in November 361. As sole emperor Julian proclaimed toleration, restored temples and sacrifices, tried to organise a pagan clergy on the Christian model, barred Christians from teaching classical literature (362), and began rebuilding the Temple in Jerusalem to falsify Christian prophecy. His reign lasted twenty months. Invading Persia with some 65,000 men in 363, he reached Ctesiphon but could not take it, retreated, and was killed in a skirmish on 26 June. His successor [[jovian|Jovian]], a Christian officer, bought the army's escape by surrendering Nisibis, Singara and the territories beyond the Tigris won in 298.

After Jovian's sudden death in 364 the army chose [[valentinian_i|Valentinian I]], a Pannonian officer, who made his brother [[valens|Valens]] emperor in the East and divided the army and court between them. Valentinian spent his reign on the Rhine and upper Danube, building and repairing forts, and died of a stroke in 375 while berating envoys of the Quadi. In the East, Valens survived the usurpation of Procopius (365-366), fought the Goths (367-369), and then faced a new situation. The Huns, nomadic horsemen from the steppe, destroyed the Gothic kingdom of the Greuthungi north of the Black Sea around 375, and in 376 the Tervingi under Fritigern asked to cross the Danube and settle within the empire. Valens agreed, needing recruits, but the reception was mismanaged by corrupt officials; starving refugees sold their children for dog meat, according to Ammianus. The Goths revolted. On 9 August 378, at [[battle_of_adrianople_378|Adrianople]], Valens attacked without waiting for his nephew [[gratian|Gratian]]'s western army; he and perhaps two-thirds of the eastern field army died. Ammianus compared it to Cannae.

Gratian appointed [[theodosius_i|Theodosius]], son of a disgraced general, as eastern emperor in 379. Unable to destroy the Goths, Theodosius made a treaty in 382 allowing them to settle in Thrace as a people under their own leaders, obliged to fight for Rome: a departure from previous practice whose significance is debated. Theodosius was a convinced Nicene Christian. His edict of 380 (Cunctos populos) required all subjects to follow the faith of the bishops of Rome and Alexandria; the Council of Constantinople (381) reaffirmed and extended the Nicene creed. In the West Gratian refused the title pontifex maximus and in 382 removed the Altar of Victory again and withdrew state funding from the pagan cults and the Vestals. The prefect of Rome, Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, appealed in 384 for its restoration in a dignified petition ('we cannot reach so great a mystery by one road alone'), and Ambrose, bishop of Milan, demolished it.

Ambrose, a former governor turned bishop in 374, embodies the new power of the episcopate. He faced down the empress Justina over a church for the Arians in 386, forced Theodosius to cancel an order to rebuild a synagogue burned by Christians at Callinicum (388), and excluded him from communion after the massacre of some 7,000 people at Thessalonica in 390 until he did public penance. Theodosius' laws of 391-392 banned sacrifice and visits to temples entirely; in 391 the bishop Theophilus and a Christian crowd destroyed the Serapeum of Alexandria. When the Frankish general Arbogast set up the rhetorician Eugenius as western emperor in 392, the pagan aristocrat Virius Nicomachus Flavianus rallied to him; Theodosius defeated them at the [[battle_of_frigidus|Frigidus]] in September 394, helped by a wind that Christian writers claimed blew the enemy's arrows back on them. He died in Milan on 17 January 395, leaving the East to [[arcadius|Arcadius]] and the West to [[honorius|Honorius]], both young, under guardians.

The Christianisation of the empire was a social as much as a political process. Christians may have formed perhaps 10 per cent of the population in 300 and a majority by 400 (the estimates are speculative). The church acquired wealth through imperial and private gifts, and bishops became urban patrons, judges and spokesmen. Monasticism, born in Egypt with Antony and Pachomius, spread through Syria, Palestine and, via writers like Athanasius and Jerome, to the West; ascetic aristocrats such as Melania the Elder and Paula founded monasteries in the Holy Land. Pilgrimage, the cult of martyrs and relics, and new church buildings remade urban space. Yet traditional culture persisted: the senatorial aristocracy of Rome, with its vast estates in Italy, Sicily and Africa, kept its classical education and much of its paganism into the 380s, and Christian aristocrats adopted the same literary culture. Alan Cameron has argued that the image of a militant 'pagan revival' in the Roman senate is largely a modern invention.

Economically, the fourth century was in many regions prosperous. The gold solidus underpinned a fiscal system that paid the army in coin and in kind; great villas in Spain, Sicily (Piazza Armerina) and Britain reached their peak; and the eastern provinces, especially Syria and Palestine, saw rising rural population. The burden of taxation and the hereditary obligations placed on decurions and some trades (laws tied coloni to the land and sons to their fathers' occupations) indicate the state's needs more than a reality of universal compulsion. At its end the empire was still strong, but it now faced a new kind of problem: armed peoples established inside its borders.
chapters.historiography: The fourth century has been central to debates on Christianisation. Older narratives of 'triumph' (Eusebius) or 'decline' (Gibbon) have given way to studies of a negotiated religious change: Brown on the holy man, the bishop and the aristocracy; MacMullen on the persistence of paganism and the role of coercion; Cameron on the myth of a late pagan revival; Salzman on aristocratic conversion. Ammianus' reliability and his own religious stance (Matthews, Barnes, Kelly) shape our view of Julian, Valentinian and Adrianople. The Gothic treaty of 382 is read either as the first creation of an autonomous barbarian state within the empire (Heather) or as a conventional settlement (Errington). Lenski's study of Valens and Matthews's work on western aristocracies remain essential.
reading: Matthews, The Roman Empire of Ammianus (1989)
Matthews, Western Aristocracies and Imperial Court AD 364-425 (1975)
Lenski, Failure of Empire: Valens and the Roman State in the Fourth Century AD (2002)
Brown, The Rise of Western Christendom (2nd ed. 2003)
Cameron, The Last Pagans of Rome (2011)
MacMullen, Christianizing the Roman Empire AD 100-400 (1984)
Bowersock, Julian the Apostate (1978)

chapters.title: The End of the Western Empire
chapters.body:
Between the death of Theodosius in 395 and the death of Odoacer in 493, the western half of the Roman empire ceased to exist as a political unit. In its place stood kingdoms ruled by Gothic, Vandal, Frankish, Burgundian and Suevic kings, most of them governing Roman populations through Roman officials and Roman law. The eastern empire, governed from Constantinople, survived intact. Why the West fell and the East did not, and whether 'fall' is even the right word, is the oldest question in the field.

The western court after 395 was dominated by generals. [[stilicho|Stilicho]], half-Vandal, married to Theodosius' niece Serena and father-in-law of the emperor [[honorius|Honorius]], held supreme command for thirteen years. His policy was compromised by rivalry with Constantinople over Illyricum and by the problem of [[alaric_i|Alaric]], leader of the Goths settled in 382, who wanted a Roman command, pay and land for his people. Stilicho fought Alaric at Pollentia (402) and Verona but never destroyed him, preferring to use him. In 405-406 a Gothic army under Radagaisus invaded Italy and was annihilated at Faesulae; on the last day of 406 (or perhaps 405) Vandals, Alans and Sueves crossed the Rhine and ravaged Gaul, and the army in Britain proclaimed Constantine III, who crossed to Gaul. In 408 Stilicho was executed on Honorius' orders, and Roman troops massacred the families of barbarian soldiers in Italy, driving thousands to Alaric.

Alaric besieged Rome three times. After the city paid a vast ransom (5,000 pounds of gold, 30,000 of silver, 4,000 silk robes, 3,000 scarlet-dyed skins and 3,000 pounds of pepper) and negotiations with Honorius, safe behind the marshes of Ravenna, failed, the Goths entered Rome on 24 August 410 and sacked it for three days. The physical damage was limited and churches were respected; the shock was immense. Jerome wrote from Bethlehem that the city which had taken the whole world was itself taken; Augustine began the City of God to answer pagans who blamed the abandonment of the gods. Alaric died weeks later. His brother-in-law Athaulf led the Goths into Gaul and married Honorius' half-sister Galla Placidia ([[galla_placidia|Galla Placidia]]), captured in Rome.

The general Constantius restored order between 411 and 421. He defeated Constantine III, starved the Goths into a treaty and used them against the Vandals and Alans in Spain, and in 418 settled them in Aquitaine, the core of what became the Visigothic kingdom of Toulouse. The terms of settlement, whether grants of land or shares of tax revenue, are fiercely debated. Constantius married Placidia and was briefly co-emperor before his death in 421. After Honorius died in 423 and a usurper was removed by an eastern army, Placidia ruled as regent for her six-year-old son [[valentinian_iii|Valentinian III]] (425-455), while generals fought for power.

The decisive blow was the loss of Africa. In 429 the Vandal king [[gaiseric|Gaiseric]] crossed from Spain with perhaps 80,000 people. Hippo fell in 431 after a siege during which Augustine died; a treaty in 435 gave the Vandals Numidia and Mauretania; in October 439 Gaiseric took Carthage. Africa had been the West's richest tax base and the source of Rome's grain. The western government's revenue, already reduced by the loss of much of Spain and Gaul to the control of barbarian groups, now collapsed; laws of the 440s cut tax remissions and imposed new levies, and the army could no longer be paid at strength. A joint East-West expedition against Carthage was abandoned in 441 because of the Huns.

[[aetius|Flavius Aetius]], who had spent years as a hostage among the Huns, dominated the West from 433 to 454. He used Hunnic auxiliaries to crush the Burgundians on the Rhine (436-437) and Bacaudae in Gaul. When [[attila|Attila]], who ruled the Huns and their subject peoples from the Hungarian plain and extracted thousands of pounds of gold from Constantinople in the 440s, turned west in 451, Aetius assembled a coalition of Romans, Visigoths, Franks and Burgundians and fought him to a standstill at the [[battle_of_catalaunian_plains|Catalaunian Plains]] in Champagne. Attila invaded Italy in 452, destroyed Aquileia, and withdrew after meeting an embassy led by Pope Leo I, more likely because of disease and supply problems. He died in 453; his empire disintegrated after the battle of Nedao (454). In September 454 Valentinian III personally killed Aetius; six months later Aetius' retainers killed Valentinian, ending the Theodosian dynasty in the West. In June 455 Gaiseric's fleet sailed to Rome and sacked it for two weeks, more thoroughly than Alaric, carrying off Valentinian's widow and daughters.

The last twenty years were the age of the generalissimo [[ricimer|Ricimer]], of Suevic and Visigothic royal descent, who made and unmade emperors. Avitus (455-456), a Gallic aristocrat backed by the Visigoths, was deposed; [[majorian|Majorian]] (457-461), the last energetic western emperor, recovered southern Gaul and prepared an invasion of Africa, but the Vandals destroyed his fleet near Cartagena in 460, and Ricimer executed him. The puppet Libius Severus followed. In 467 the eastern emperor Leo I sent Anthemius to rule the West, and in 468 a vast joint expedition against the Vandals, costing perhaps 64,000 pounds of gold and 700,000 of silver, was destroyed by fireships off Cape Bon. Its failure ended any hope of recovering Africa. Ricimer killed Anthemius in 472 and died weeks later. Glycerius, Julius Nepos and finally Romulus Augustus, the child of the general Orestes, followed in rapid succession. In August 476 the barbarian soldiers in Italy, refused a third of the land, proclaimed their officer [[odoacer|Odoacer]] king. He killed Orestes, pensioned off [[romulus_augustulus|Romulus Augustulus]] in Campania, and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople, asking to rule Italy as the emperor's representative. Nepos, the last emperor recognised by the East, lived in Dalmatia until 480.

Contemporaries did not see 476 as an epoch; the Roman Senate continued to meet, consuls were still named, and Odoacer governed through Roman officials. In 488 the eastern emperor [[zeno|Zeno]] encouraged the Ostrogothic king [[theodoric_the_great|Theodoric]] to march on Italy. After defeats on the Isonzo, at Verona and on the Adda, Odoacer held out in Ravenna until 493, when Theodoric killed him with his own hands at a banquet. Theodoric's thirty-three-year reign would be remembered by Italians as a golden age of Roman civilisation under a Gothic king. Meanwhile [[clovis_i|Clovis]], king of the Franks, ended the last Roman enclave in northern Gaul at Soissons in 486.

Why did the West fall? Peter Heather emphasises an external shock: the Huns pushed new groups into the empire and then, through their own empire, created larger, more formidable confederations; the loss of tax base to these groups, culminating in Africa, made the western state unviable. Guy Halsall stresses internal politics: Roman factional conflict drew in barbarian forces, and the withdrawal of central authority from the provinces led local elites to accommodate new rulers. Walter Goffart argued that settlement was a relatively peaceful 'accommodation' managed by Roman officials, often through tax shares. Bryan Ward-Perkins, against the fashion for 'transformation', demonstrated an archaeological catastrophe in the West: the collapse of pottery production and trade, of coinage, of building in stone, even of the size of cattle, to levels below the Iron Age. The East survived because it was richer, its capital impregnable behind the Theodosian walls (413), its frontier with Persia mostly quiet, and its rulers able to buy off or divert enemies westward.
chapters.historiography: Gibbon's 'triumph of barbarism and religion' framed the debate for two centuries. The 'transformation of the Roman world' school (Brown, the European Science Foundation project of the 1990s, Goffart, Pohl) emphasised continuity, ethnogenesis and accommodation, and the constructed nature of 'barbarian' identities (the Vienna school of Wolfram and Pohl; critique by Goffart and Gillett). Heather and Ward-Perkins (both 2005) reasserted violent fall and material collapse; Halsall offered a synthesis focused on Roman politics and the frontier regions; Wickham's Framing the Early Middle Ages made fiscal structures and aristocratic wealth the key variables. Kulikowski challenged the scale of migration and the idea of coherent Gothic peoples entering the empire. The hospitalitas debate (land versus tax shares) is unresolved.
reading: Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)
Halsall, Barbarian Migrations and the Roman West 376-568 (2007)
Ward-Perkins, The Fall of Rome and the End of Civilization (2005)
Goffart, Barbarians and Romans AD 418-584 (1980)
Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)
Wickham, Framing the Early Middle Ages (2005)
MacGeorge, Late Roman Warlords (2002)

chapters.title: Justinian and the Eastern Empire
chapters.body:
The eastern Roman empire around 500 was the richest and most populous state in western Eurasia. It held the Balkans, Asia Minor, Syria, Palestine and Egypt, with cities like Antioch, Alexandria and Constantinople (perhaps 400,000 to 500,000 people) at its core. Its rulers called themselves and their subjects Romans; 'Byzantine' is a sixteenth-century coinage. Under Anastasius I ([[anastasius_i|Anastasius]], 491-518), a former palace official, prudent finance (abolition of the chrysargyron in 498, reform of the copper coinage, collection of taxes in gold) left a reserve of 320,000 pounds of gold, Procopius says. It also left a bitter religious division. Since the Council of Chalcedon (451) defined Christ as one person in two natures, much of Egypt and Syria had rejected the definition in favour of a single, united nature (the Miaphysites); Anastasius leaned towards them, provoking riots in Constantinople and the revolt of the general Vitalian (513-515).

[[justin_i|Justin I]] (518-527), an illiterate peasant from near Naissus who rose to command the palace guard, restored Chalcedonian orthodoxy and reunion with Rome. Real power increasingly lay with his nephew Justinian ([[justinian_i|Justinian]]), whom he adopted and who succeeded him in 527. Justinian married [[theodora|Theodora]], a former actress and daughter of a bear-keeper in the Hippodrome, after Justin changed the law forbidding senators to marry actresses. Their partnership, the subject of Procopius' scabrous Secret History, was political as well as personal: Theodora protected the Miaphysites while Justinian sought compromise.

The reign's first great project was legal. Between 528 and 534 a commission led by Tribonian produced the Code (a collection of imperial constitutions, first edition 529, second 534), the Digest or Pandects (533), which condensed some two thousand books of classical jurists into fifty, and the Institutes (533), a textbook for students. Justinian's later laws, the Novels, were mostly issued in Greek. Together, as the Corpus Iuris Civilis, they became the foundation of civil law in continental Europe after their rediscovery in eleventh-century Bologna.

In January 532 the circus factions of the Blues and Greens, usually rivals, united against the emperor's ministers in the Nika riot, burned much of the city centre including the church of Hagia Sophia, and proclaimed a rival emperor. Justinian prepared to flee; Procopius gives Theodora a speech declaring that royalty makes a good burial shroud. The generals [[belisarius|Belisarius]] and Mundus trapped the crowd in the Hippodrome and killed, by the usual figure, 30,000. Within six weeks Justinian began rebuilding Hagia Sophia, designed by Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, with a dome 31 metres across; it was dedicated on 27 December 537.

War with Persia dominated the reign's first and last decades. Belisarius won at Dara (530) but lost at Callinicum (531); the accession of [[khosrow_i|Khosrow I]] allowed an 'Eternal Peace' in 532, purchased for 11,000 pounds of gold. This freed Justinian for the West. In 533 Belisarius sailed against the Vandal kingdom with about 15,000 soldiers; he won at Ad Decimum (13 September) and Tricamarum, took Carthage, and returned in 534 with the Vandal king Gelimer and the treasure of the Jerusalem Temple, looted by Titus and taken by Gaiseric from Rome, for a triumph in the Hippodrome. Africa was restored to the empire within a year, though Berber wars and military mutinies troubled it for over a decade.

Italy proved far harder. The murder of the Ostrogothic queen Amalasuntha, Theodoric's daughter, in 535 gave Justinian his pretext. The [[gothic_war_535|Gothic War]] lasted, with intervals, until 554. Belisarius took Sicily, Naples and Rome (536), withstood a year-long siege by the Gothic king Witigis (537-538), and took Ravenna in 540. But in 540 Khosrow broke the peace, sacked Antioch and deported its people to a new city near Ctesiphon, and Belisarius was recalled. In Italy the new Gothic king [[totila|Totila]] (541-552) reconquered most of the peninsula, besieged and twice took Rome, and freed slaves and coloni to fight. The eunuch general [[narses|Narses]], with a large army including Lombard and Herul mercenaries, defeated and killed Totila at Busta Gallorum (Taginae) in 552, and the last Gothic king Teia at Mons Lactarius near Vesuvius. The Pragmatic Sanction of 554 restored Roman administration, but Italy had been devastated by two decades of war; Rome may have shrunk to a few tens of thousands of people. A foothold in south-eastern Spain was taken from the Visigoths in 552.

Between these campaigns came catastrophe. In 541 bubonic plague, now confirmed by ancient DNA from burials to be Yersinia pestis, reached Pelusium in Egypt and in spring 542 Constantinople, where Procopius claims 10,000 a day died at the peak; John of Ephesus describes corpses stacked in towers. It recurred in waves for two centuries. Its demographic effect is contested: some historians see a collapse comparable to the Black Death that undermined the fiscal and military base for the rest of the century; others, pointing to continued building, coinage and documentary activity, argue for a smaller impact. A volcanic 'dust veil' in 536, attested by Procopius and Cassiodorus and now by ice cores and tree rings, began a period of colder climate (the Late Antique Little Ice Age) that may have compounded the strain.

Religious policy was Justinian's other obsession. He closed the funding of the philosophical schools of Athens (529), persecuted pagans, Manichaeans, Samaritans (whose revolt of 529 was crushed) and heretics, and sought a formula to reconcile Miaphysites to Chalcedon. His condemnation of the 'Three Chapters', writings of three dead theologians offensive to Miaphysites, was imposed at the Fifth Ecumenical Council (553) and on the reluctant Pope Vigilius, who had been brought to Constantinople; it failed to win over the East and provoked schism in the West. A separate Miaphysite church hierarchy, ordained by Jacob Baradaeus with Theodora's protection, consolidated the division of eastern Christianity that the Arab conquests would make permanent.

The reign ended with the empire stretched. The Fifty Years' Peace with Persia (561/562) cost 30,000 nomismata a year. New peoples appeared on the Danube: the Kutrigur Huns reached the Long Walls of Constantinople in 559 and were repelled by the aged Belisarius, and the Avars, fleeing the Turks, made contact in 558. Justinian died on 14 November 565, aged about eighty-three. Our main source, Procopius, wrote three works with apparently contradictory views: the Wars, a classicising history; the Buildings, a panegyric; and the Secret History, an invective portraying Justinian as a demon. Reconciling them is the key problem of the period. Whether Justinian's reconquests were a grand strategy of restoration, achievable but blighted by plague, or a fatal overextension that left the East exposed, remains the central question of his reign.
chapters.historiography: Interpretation of Justinian depends on Procopius: Cameron read him as a conventional classicising historian, Kaldellis as a subversive critic using classical allusion to attack autocracy. Evans, Maas's Cambridge Companion and Meier's work survey the reign; Sarris analysed the great estates of Egypt (the Apion family) and the conflict between state and aristocracy. The plague debate opposes maximalists (Little's volume, Harper, Meier) to minimalists (Mordechai, Eisenberg and others, 2019). Greatrex and Lieu document the Persian wars; the 'reconquest' is evaluated variously as ideologically driven restoration or opportunism.
reading: Maas (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to the Age of Justinian (2005)
Evans, The Age of Justinian (1996)
Kaldellis, Procopius of Caesarea: Tyranny, History, and Philosophy at the End of Antiquity (2004)
Cameron, Procopius and the Sixth Century (1985)
Sarris, Economy and Society in the Age of Justinian (2006)
Little (ed.), Plague and the End of Antiquity (2007)
Greatrex and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars, Part II, AD 363-630 (2002)

chapters.title: Heraclius and the End of Antiquity
chapters.body:
The last three-quarters of a century of this history saw the Roman empire fight the longest and most destructive war in its history against Persia, win it against all expectation, and then lose its richest provinces within a decade to a new power from Arabia. By 641, when Heraclius died, the empire was a different state: Greek-speaking, centred on Constantinople, Anatolia and the Aegean, organised for permanent defence. Many historians date the end of antiquity to these years.

Justin II (565-578), Justinian's nephew, began by refusing to pay subsidies to the Avars and Persians, a policy of honour that proved disastrous. In 568 the Lombards, displaced from Pannonia by the Avars, invaded Italy and within a few years held the north and much of the centre and south (the duchies of Spoleto and Benevento), leaving the empire coastal enclaves around Ravenna, Rome and Naples. War with Persia resumed in 572 over Armenia; in 573 Khosrow I took the great fortress of Dara, and Justin went mad. His wife Sophia and the general Tiberius governed; Tiberius II (578-582) spent lavishly. Maurice ([[maurice|Maurice]], 582-602), a capable soldier-administrator, attributed with the military manual called the Strategikon, made the empire's position recover. When the Persian king Khosrow II ([[khosrow_ii|Khosrow II]]) was overthrown in 590, Maurice restored him with a Roman army and in return received most of Armenia and Iberia (591). He then turned to the Balkans, where the Avar khaganate, which had taken Sirmium in 582, and Slavic groups had been raiding and settling, and from 592 campaigned north of the Danube with some success. Maurice created the exarchates of Ravenna and Carthage, combining civil and military authority in distant provinces. But economy measures, especially an order in 602 that the army winter north of the Danube, provoked a mutiny. The centurion Phocas ([[phocas|Phocas]]) marched on Constantinople, and Maurice and his sons were executed.

Khosrow II used the murder of his benefactor as a pretext for war in 603. The Persian offensive of 603-622 was the greatest military disaster in Roman history. Dara fell in 604; Roman Mesopotamia and Armenia were overrun. Phocas' reign of terror was ended in 610 by Heraclius ([[heraclius|Heraclius]]), son of the exarch of Africa, who sailed from Carthage and had Phocas executed. Heraclius inherited collapse. The Persians took Antioch (613), Damascus, and in 614 Jerusalem, where they killed or enslaved thousands and carried off the relic of the True Cross to Ctesiphon. Egypt fell in 618-621, cutting the free grain supply of Constantinople, which was ended in 618. Persian armies reached Chalcedon, across the Bosporus. In the Balkans the Avars and Slavs overran much of the peninsula, and Greek cities from Sirmium to the Peloponnese were destroyed or isolated. Heraclius halved military pay, melted down church plate, and considered moving the capital to Carthage.

From 622 Heraclius took the field in person, an act without precedent since Theodosius I. Rather than attack the Persian armies in Syria and Asia Minor, he struck through Armenia and the Caucasus at the Persian heartland, campaigning in 624-626 in Atropatene, where he destroyed the great fire temple at Takht-i Suleiman. In 626 the Avars, Slavs and a Persian army under Shahrbaraz besieged Constantinople from both sides of the Bosporus; the defence, led by the patriarch Sergius and the patrician Bonus while the emperor was absent, held, and the Slavic boats were destroyed in the Golden Horn. The citizens credited the Virgin. Allied with the Western Turks, Heraclius invaded Mesopotamia and defeated the Persian army at [[battle_of_nineveh_627|Nineveh]] in December 627. Khosrow II was overthrown and killed in February 628; his son Kavadh II made peace, returning all Roman territory and the Cross. Heraclius restored the True Cross to Jerusalem in March 630 (629 on some reckonings), the triumphant culmination of what had been presented as a holy war. After 629 he adopted the Greek title basileus in official documents in place of the Latin imperator and Augustus.

The victory was hollow. Both empires were exhausted, the Roman provinces of the East had been under Persian administration for up to two decades, and the Persian state descended into civil war. In the same years a new monotheistic movement had united the tribes of Arabia under the prophet [[muhammad|Muhammad]] (died 632) and his successors. Arab forces raided southern Palestine from 633-634. Under the caliph [[umar|Umar]] they defeated Roman forces at Ajnadayn (634), took Damascus (635), and destroyed the main Roman field army on the [[battle_of_yarmuk|Yarmuk]] in August 636, a battle in which Arab mobility and Roman disunity (Armenian and Arab Christian contingents quarrelled with Roman commanders) proved decisive. Heraclius abandoned Syria, reportedly bidding it farewell from the Taurus. Jerusalem surrendered to Umar in 637 or 638. The Persian empire collapsed in the same years at al-Qadisiyya (636 or 637) and Nahavand (642). In 639-640 Amr ibn al-As invaded Egypt; the fortress of Babylon fell in 641 and Alexandria by treaty in 642.

Religious division contributed to the speed of these losses, though less than older historians claimed. Heraclius and the patriarch Sergius sought to reconcile Miaphysites with a doctrine of a single energy (monenergism) and then a single will (monotheletism) in Christ, proclaimed in the Ekthesis of 638. It satisfied neither side and provoked opposition in the West led by Maximus the Confessor and the popes. The Christians of Syria and Egypt did not, for the most part, welcome the Arabs, but many had little reason to fight for Constantinople, and the conquerors' terms (tribute and toleration) were often lighter than those of the Persian occupiers.

Heraclius died on 11 February 641, leaving the succession to his sons [[constantine_iii_heraclius|Constantine III]] and [[heraclonas|Heraclonas]], whose quarrels and early deaths soon led to the accession of Constans II. The empire they inherited had lost Syria, Palestine and, within a year, Egypt, which had provided perhaps a third of its revenues. What remained, Anatolia, the Aegean islands, parts of the Balkans, Sicily, North Africa and enclaves in Italy, had to be reorganised for survival. In the following decades the field armies were settled in the provinces of Asia Minor, the origin of the 'themes'; cities contracted to fortified citadels (kastra); coinage and trade shrank; and the late Roman aristocracy gave way to a service elite. Latin disappeared from administration. The state that emerged, which modern historians call Byzantine, still called itself Roman and would last until 1453.

Where then does Roman antiquity end? Henri Pirenne argued that the unity of the Mediterranean, the essential condition of ancient civilisation, survived the Germanic kingdoms and was broken only by the Arab conquests: 'without Muhammad, Charlemagne would be inconceivable'. Peter Brown placed the end of 'late antiquity' in a long seventh or even eighth century. Whatever the label, the generation of Heraclius saw the end of the political structure that had united the Mediterranean since the Punic Wars: Rome, Persia and the classical city, which had defined this history since 509 BC, gave way to the Caliphate, a reduced Christian Roman empire, and the kingdoms of the Latin West.
chapters.historiography: The seventh century is poorly documented in Greek narrative (Theophylact Simocatta ends in 602; the Chronicon Paschale ends in 628; Theophanes and Nikephoros wrote two centuries later) and must be reconstructed from Armenian (Sebeos), Syriac, Coptic and Arabic sources and from documents, seals, coins and archaeology. Howard-Johnston's Witnesses to a World Crisis assesses this source base; Kaegi's biography and Haldon's Byzantium in the Seventh Century are standard. Debates concern the origins of the theme system (Heraclian reform, as Ostrogorsky argued, or a gradual later development, as most now believe), the impact of plague and climate, the role of religious dissent in the conquests, and the nature of early Islam and its sources (Donner, Hoyland). Pirenne's thesis has been reassessed in the light of archaeology (Hodges and Whitehouse, McCormick, Wickham), which suggests Mediterranean trade had contracted well before the Arabs.
reading: Kaegi, Heraclius: Emperor of Byzantium (2003)
Haldon, Byzantium in the Seventh Century (rev. ed. 1997)
Howard-Johnston, Witnesses to a World Crisis (2010)
Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and his Historian (1988)
Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992)
Hoyland, In God's Path: The Arab Conquests and the Creation of an Islamic Empire (2015)
Sarris, Empires of Faith: The Fall of Rome to the Rise of Islam, 500-700 (2011)
